analysis.one_liner: Creates an FTC cybersecurity office to police and penalize credit reporting agencies for data breaches.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in May 2019, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: After massive breaches exposed millions of Americans' Social Security numbers and financial data, this bill would have created a new Office of Cybersecurity inside the Federal Trade Commission to write mandatory security rules for the big credit reporting agencies, examine them annually, and investigate violations. It would have required agencies to report breaches to the FTC within 10 days and notify affected consumers, and it would have imposed automatic civil penalties — $100 per consumer whose name and another piece of identifying data was exposed, plus $50 per additional exposed item — with half the money going to breach victims and half to the new office. It also would have closed a gap in the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act so nationwide credit reporting agencies count as 'financial institutions' for privacy enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose Social Security numbers, driver's licenses, and financial account numbers sit in credit bureau databases. Stricter security standards, mandatory breach disclosure within 10 days, and automatic per-consumer penalties paid half to victims would make breaches costlier for the agencies and give affected people some compensation. Law enforcement and intelligence agencies would also get prompt notice of breaches.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose data credit bureaus hold

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Office of Cybersecurity at the FTC that writes detailed data-security rules for credit reporting agencies — including encryption of data at rest and in transit, continuous vulnerability monitoring and patching, and data minimization — and examines each covered agency annually.

Requires a credit reporting agency to report any breach of personally identifying information to the FTC within 10 days, and to notify every affected consumer with the breach date, number of people affected, remedial steps, and potential risks.

Mandates an automatic civil penalty of $100 for each consumer whose name plus another piece of identifying data was exposed, plus $50 per additional exposed item — doubled if the agency misses the reporting deadline or violates the security rules — capped at 50% (or 75% for repeat violations) of the agency's prior-year gross revenue.

Directs that half of every penalty be divided among the consumers affected by the breach and half fund the new cybersecurity office, and explicitly preserves consumers' right to sue under state and federal law.

analysis.who_pays: The credit reporting agencies, mainly the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion), which would face new compliance costs, annual examinations, and potentially multibillion-dollar penalties after any breach. Some of those costs would likely be passed on through the price of credit reports and credit-monitoring products.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit reporting agencies and data-heavy firms

drawbacks.text: The per-consumer penalty formula is blunt: on the scale of past breaches, it could produce penalties in the tens of billions of dollars, and the bill gives courts little discretion to scale the penalty to actual harm or fault beyond the revenue caps.

Compliance costs for detailed security mandates — encryption, continuous monitoring, annual examinations — would fall on the bureaus and could be passed to consumers through higher prices for credit reports and related products, with no provision addressing that pass-through.
The bill applies only to consumer reporting agencies, leaving other companies that hold equally sensitive data — banks, retailers, health systems — outside this framework's reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is real and targeted at an industry that has repeatedly failed to safeguard the most sensitive data Americans have, including a breach affecting roughly 147 million people. The main costs are compliance spending and blunt penalty sizing, and the bill's scope is narrower than the broader data-security problem. On balance, the protections and victim compensation outweigh the acknowledged costs, and the 50% revenue cap gives even a badly breached agency a survivable ceiling.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on May 7, 2019, joined by Sen. Mark Warner as its sole cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nationwide credit reporting agencies, which avoided new security mandates, annual FTC examinations, and automatic penalties reaching up to half or three-quarters of a year's gross revenue. Consumers whose data the bureaus hold got no new federal protections or breach compensation.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create an FTC cybersecurity office and impose breach penalties on credit reporting agencies.

for.name: Sen. Mark Warner
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Held the referred bill without any hearing, markup, or vote for the remaining twenty months of the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by two Democrats and never advanced far enough for any vote, so no measure of partisan support or opposition beyond sponsorship exists in the record.

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion and other large bureaus)
industries.note: The bill targets them directly: mandatory security standards, annual FTC examinations, breach disclosure within 10 days, and automatic per-consumer penalties capped only at 50-75% of gross revenue — a direct hit to an industry whose business model is selling consumers' personal data. Its interest in the bill ran squarely against consumers', and it avoided all of it when the bill died.

The bill would have created a large compliance market — continuous monitoring, penetration testing, encryption, and annual examinations required of every covered bureau — and half of all breach penalties were earmarked for cybersecurity research and inspections. Its interest ran alongside consumers', since better-funded security is what consumers would be paying for.
